title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.Trum
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together. Asked about the president's comments, the new prime minister said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that and hence me indicating that to the president."Burnham has faced pressure from some trade unions, industry figures and some of his own Labour MPs to back increased drilling in the North Sea.In its 2024 general election manifesto, Labour promised not to issue new licences for drilling but said it would honour existing ones.As energy secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government, Ed Miliband was a staunch supporter of Labour's manifesto position. He has previously described the licence issued to Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field, as "climate vandalism".Miliband is now the foreign secretary in Burnham's government.Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government. In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil."If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country." He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank." "Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat. "Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy."It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices. Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency". Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea."Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" -  production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland. In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge. The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Level, also known as the windfall tax.

schema.headline: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil

title: Thousands evacuated in Crete as wildfires threaten tourist resorts
description: Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.Two firef
body: Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.Two firefighters died on the island on Wednesday when they became trapped while tackling a fire near Krya Vrysi in the Rethymno region. A third firefighter died on the Greek mainland, near the port town of Gytheio in the Peloponnese. As gusts reached 125km/h (77mph) on the island, around 8,000 people were evacuated from their homes overnight but were later allowed to return.Greece is among many European countries facing devastating fires and drought. Several fires have continued to burn in Spain and Portugal, although Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared an end to the national emergency for wildfires in the Ávila and Madrid regions.In south-west France some residents have been able to return to their homes after a major wildfire in the Gironde region.The fire raging in Crete broke out in the Rethymno region on Wednesday and has since spread rapidly, destroying homes and agricultural land. It remains one of the biggest fires currently active on the island and is still burning out of control.There was no clear picture of the destruction so far, Rethymno's deputy regional governor Maria Lioni said, adding that containing the fire was the main priority.Lioni described Wednesday as a "dark day" for the region and said gusts overnight reached up to 11 on the Beaufort scale - a wind force categorised as "violent" - fanning the flames and hampering containment efforts.Some of those evacuated in Rethymno were moved into a temporary shelter."I was watching the fire and I just didn't know what to do. It was like a volcano down the side of the mountain," said Bianca Boorer, who was visiting the coastal resort of Agios Pavlos with her mother on a yoga retreat."The bar staff told us you need to get in cars and drive away but only two people had cars. Eleven people tried to get into one tiny car and the car my mum was in was nearer to the fire," she told the BBC's Your Voice."The place we had breakfast in has burnt down. Agios Pavlos hotel has burnt down, the place we did yoga in has also burnt down."Meanwhile, wildfires have erupted in the north-western Spanish provinces of Zamora and León, not far from the border with Portugal, with more than 1,000 people evacuated.Five people were injured in a fire in the eastern town of Valpaços in Portugal, according to local reports.A major fire that consumed an area in excess of 66,000 hectares to the west of the Spanish capital, Madrid, and caused tens of thousands of people to be evacuated has stopped spreading, allowing some residents to return home.As he ended the national emergency in the area, Pedro Sánchez urged "extreme caution" during the fourth heatwave of the summer in Spain.The fire in Ávila, which has burned more than 43,000 hectares over the past week, is now considered the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history. A small amount of rain fell near Bordeaux in France on Thursday, raising hopes that the Gironde wildfire that has burned an area larger than the US city of Detroit and destroyed 240 homes might soon be over.The region's fire service said it was "reasonably optimistic" given that the fire had not grown in size since the weekend.Around 84,000 of the 220,000 displaced residents were allowed to return home on Thursday, according to French reports.It is estimated that more than 90,000 hectares of land across France have burnt this year - higher than any other year on record, according to data from the European Forest Fire Information Service.In Spain, more than 200,000 hectares have burnt in 2026 – roughly five times above the average for the time of year. The area of land ravaged in Portugal is also higher than usual for this point in July.The European fire season typically extends into August and September – and with more hot weather on the way in the coming days, these figures are likely to keep rising.Most wildfires are started by humans, whether deliberately or accidentally, but climate change is strengthening weather conditions conducive to fires spreading.Last winter was mild and wet, encouraging vegetation growth, which has then dried out in successive heatwaves, generating tinder-dry fuel for wildfires.Some researchers have also warned that the Mediterranean's forests and scrublands are not being properly managed – leaving plenty of vegetation as fuel for fires.Forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected.In Turkey, hundreds of homes have also been evacuated but the majority of fires that have broken out mainly in the south have been brought under control, authorities say.If you are affected and it is safe to do so, please get in touch by using this link or the form below.

schema.headline: Thousands evacuated in Crete as wildfires threaten tourist resorts

title: Missile that left crater deep inside Poland was probably Russian - Polish PM Tusk
description: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday was "in all probabilit
body: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday was "in all probability" a Russian cruise missile, and it was armed.It left a10m-wide (33ft) crater a short distance from the village of Tarnawa Kolonia, 92km (57 miles) from the border with Ukraine during a large-scale Russian attack on the cities of Lviv, Kyiv and near Kryvyhi Rih.Tusk said initially that "all the indications" were that the missile that violated Polish airspace was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, during a specially convened meeting in the eastern city of Lublin.He then went to the site of the incident and said that according to military experts the majority of "recovered fragments point to it being a Russian Kh-101 missile".Although no casualties had been reported in Thursday's incident near Tarnawa Kolonia, the Polish prime minister made clear it was being taken very seriously. There was no immediate threat as it had not landed in a built-up area, he said, adding that "we were prepared to shoot it down if had continued its flight".Nato said it was in close contact with Polish authorities and the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, Gen Alexus G Grynkewich, said the Western defensive alliance would "continue to take all necessary measures to defend Nato territory".Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said about 20 objects were seen close to Polish airspace overnight and pyrotechnical analysis was being carried out.Ukraine's acting Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha had earlier declared definitively that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had "crossed into Poland as part of Russia's massive strike against Ukraine, violating Nato airspace".Tusk said he was in contact with fellow European leaders and the head of the European Council António Costa said Russia's "massive combined strike against Ukraine" had underlined again that "Russia's aggression is a threat to the security as a whole". At least eight people died and dozens more were wounded across Ukraine, including six members of one family in a village near Kryvyih Rih. Dozens more were wounded in Lviv, not far from Ukraine's western border with Poland.A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine began in February 2022. Two Polish farmers were killed by a missile that landed just over the border from Ukraine in November 2022, but that was believed to have been a Ukrainian air defence missile responding to a Russian attack.Poland's military detected the object at about 03:40 on Thursday (01:40 GMT) and sent an F-16 fighter jet to intercept it before it disappeared minutes later from radar systems. A military helicopter was then sent to search the area.Air raid sirens blared in Lublin and Krasnystaw further to the south-east because of the Russian airstrikes in neighbouring Ukraine. Residents in Tarnawa Kolonia reported hearing a loud bang at about 04:00 and police found the crash site about an hour later.The Polish leader had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Lublin the previous evening as Zelensky was returning from talks with US President Donald Trump.

schema.headline: Missile that left crater deep inside Poland was probably Russian - Polish PM Tusk

title: Prison recalls up 28% in England and Wales, new figures reveal
description: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures revealByTom Edgington and Harriet AgerholmBBC VerifyThere has been a large rise in the number of
body: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures revealByTom Edgington and Harriet AgerholmBBC VerifyThere has been a large rise in the number of offenders being recalled to prisons in England and Wales having been released on licence, new government figures show.There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.The figures follow government schemes to release a number of offenders early in an effort to ease prison overcrowding.The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said offenders released on licence face strict conditions "and can be hauled back to prison if they break these rules".Cassia Rowland, from the Institute for Government think tank, said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public."The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.The most common reason provided for prison recalls between January and March was "non-compliance" (9,683), followed by "failed to keep in touch" (5,025).There were 2,891 recalls because an offender faced further charges between January and March 2026, a 23% rise on the same period in 2025. More than one reason can be recorded against each recall.Alex Hewson, from the Prison Reform Trust, said: "Many leave prison facing challenges such as addiction, poor mental health and unstable housing, making compliance with licence conditions difficult."Responding to the figures, the MOJ said "public protection is our priority" and the statistics "show that we do not hesitate to recall offenders to prison when the risk escalates."Sentencing Act release scheme pausedThe increase in prisoner recall comes after the government introduced an early release scheme in England and Wales to help ease overcrowding pressure in September 2024.The scheme meant eligible prisoners could be released after serving 40% of their sentence rather than half.As of March 2026, 70,066 people had been released under the scheme, external.Rowland says early release schemes have contributed to the increase in recalls."But these schemes have also made it harder for prisons and probation to prepare people for release effectively and give them support with basic things like finding accommodation, accessing job support and so on."Despite the releases there were still 86,267 people in England and Wales' prisons, external as of 27 July, meaning the prison estate was 97% full.In a further attempt to ease prison capacity pressure, Sir Keir Starmer's government had planned to release some offenders after serving just one-third of their custodial term.The Sentencing Act release scheme was due to come into force from 2 September, but it has been paused by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham following criticism from survivors and victims' families.The BBC understands around 700 prisoners would have been eligible for early release under the scheme's first phase.Although the prison population has remained relatively stable since 2010, following rapid growth in the 1990s, government projections, external suggest it could rise to about 90,000 in 2028.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Burnham has announced a pause to the Sentencing Act early release schemeUsing early release to manage prison overcrowding is not new.Governments led by Labour and the Conservatives have each introduced emergency measures when the prison system has come under strain.In October 2023, Rishi Sunak's Conservative government began releasing eligible offenders up to 18 days early. The scheme was eventually expanded to up to 70 days ahead of offenders' release date.Nick Hardwick, the former chief inspector of prisons, says early release alone will not solve the problem, arguing "it's just going to slow the rate of growth".New prison plansThe Starmer government announced a plan to add 14,000 new prison places by 2031, external, including four new prisons. It said it would acquire land if necessary and would "make sure the supply always keeps up with demand".The MOJ previously told BBC Verify the government had delivered about 3,200 prison places so far - 1,600 for each of their two years in office. However, this figure only covers new prison places and does not factor in those taken out of use.Hardwick says expanding the number of prisons is only part of the answer because "the one thing you can't do quickly is produce experienced staff."The prison building programme is already costing billions of pounds, he adds, leaving it up to ministers to decide how much they are prepared to spend to keep more people in prison for longer."There's no perfect solution... it's a question of what's the least bad option."Additional reporting by Isobel Cottam

schema.headline: Prison recalls up 28% in England and Wales, new figures reveal

title: The Chinese robot army transforming the UK's retail industry
description: Every time you click "buy" on an online order, the chances are that your purchase starts getting processed within minutes.Increasingly, the journey st
body: Every time you click "buy" on an online order, the chances are that your purchase starts getting processed within minutes.Increasingly, the journey starts with a squat silver floor robot gliding beneath a storage rack, lifting a shelf and carrying it across a warehouse to a waiting worker.At Geek+'s factory in the eastern Chinese city of Hefei, which the BBC visited, fleets of the robots are built and tested before being shipped to warehouses around the world.Some of Britain's biggest retailers - including Tesco, Asda and Next - now use the company's technology.By automating these repetitive journeys, Geek+ says retailers can increase picking speeds, store more goods in spaces that are hard to reach for humans, and reduce errors.Unlike traditional warehouse automation, which relies on fixed conveyor systems and permanent infrastructure, autonomous mobile robots can be deployed simply using QR code floor markers and safety fencing.Geek+, which listed in Hong Kong last year in one of the biggest robotics share sales of 2025, has become the world's largest supplier of autonomous mobile robots.The UK has struggled with weak productivity growth for more than a decade, and economists say wider adoption of robotics will be essential if businesses are to become more efficient.In its 2026 report SME Technology Adoption in the United Kingdom, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said technologies like robotics would be key to improving productivity. According to the OECD, Britain's low adoption of robotics is "surprising" given its manufacturing heritage, noting that while UK firms have embraced mature digital technologies, they lag behind in robotics and automation.That presents an opportunity for companies such as Geek+. The UK has one of Europe's largest e-commerce and logistics sectors, but many warehouses are still in the early stages of automation.Britain has already become Geek+'s biggest European market, with UK partner MotionTech deploying more than 2,000 robots across 10 warehouse sites."Customers want fast deployable solutions," says Barry Pemberton, Account Director at MotionTech. "They want high volume, high storage, fast picking... ultimately on a smaller footprint with a reduced headcount.""We seem to have a very big shortage of labour in the UK at the moment. These technologies are really important to keep businesses thriving and meet demand."The Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents almost 6 million UK workers, says robotics should be used to raise productivity and improve jobs, rather than simply cut labour costs. In its response to the government's consultation on a new AI and innovation strategy, it urged ministers to ensure workers are involved in decisions about automation and that employers invest in retraining."Working with technologists, workers and unions can help steer the UK's research and innovation towards workers' priorities for automation... avoiding job-cutting, low-productivity automation," the TUC said in its report.Robotics has become a strategic priority for Beijing under President Xi Jinping's drive to develop what he calls "new quality productive forces".With China's working-age population shrinking, policymakers increasingly see automation as essential to boosting productivity and maintaining the country's manufacturing advantage."The robotics story builds directly on China's electric vehicle ecosystem," says Kyle Chan, a researcher at the Brookings Institution.Batteries, electric motors, cameras, sensors and semiconductors developed for electric vehicles (EVs) are increasingly being used across China's robotics sector, creating what he describes as "overlapping industrial ecosystems".One company leading that crossover is Chinese EV maker XPeng, which unveiled its humanoid robot, Iron, last year. Founder He Xiaopeng says he no longer sees XPeng simply as a carmaker."We want XPeng to be a high-tech company," he told the BBC. "In the future, any car company will transform into a car and robotics company."But the business case for humanoids is less clear than it is for today's warehouse robots. If wheeled robots move goods cheaply, reliably and efficiently or robots with just arms can do the other automated tasks, what problem does a humanoid solve?Developers say factories, hospitals and offices have all been designed around people, and so they may eventually be able to work in different environments without the need to redesign workplaces around automation.But experts and developers alike agree that the current technology is not yet suitable for some repetitive tasks that require more dexterity."I don't think [humanoids] will change the landscape of the types of technology or the automation that's going to be put into place," says Pemberton. "They're definitely going to be complementary."Chinese companies already account for the vast majority of global humanoid deployments, but it may be years before they are commonplace in warehouses.For Britain, where productivity pressures and labour shortages are driving demand for automation, the country's warehouses are becoming an early testing ground for China's next major technology export.Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar

schema.headline: The Chinese robot army transforming the UK's retail industry

title: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year
description: Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.One
body: Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, local officials said, with a one-year-old child among those hurt.Seven hours later, three people were found dead aboard a small boat after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.French officials confirmed their deaths as the Home Office reported that Wednesday saw the highest number of crossings in a single day this year, with nine boats reaching the UK.Local authorities in France said the first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.The man is thought to have been in his 30s or 40s, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people aboard. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."Prime Minister Andy Burnham, speaking separately about small boat crossings on Thursday, said the UK had made "significant progress" on reducing the number of arrivals.But, asked by reporters about US President Donald Trump's remark that the UK had a "huge immigration problem", Burnham said there was much still to do "to get those numbers right down".Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the deaths were "preventable" and that the only way to save lives was "to stop the crossings completely".He said a "proper deterrent" was required, adding: "If they [migrants] know they will be quickly removed, then they will not cross in the first place."A total of 162 people died in the English Channel between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.Small-boat crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.Wednesday's 752 arrivals surpassed the year's previous daily high of 710 recorded in June, and brings the provisional total for the year to 14,128 - which is 42% lower than the number recorded by this time last year.The Home Office has said this is not just down to weather conditions but also its work with French authorities to prevent crossings by ensuring enforcement action on beaches and seizing boats, including a £662m deal signed in April.Wednesday's figure is the highest number recorded in one day since 20 December 2025, when there were 803 arrivals - but is well below the 1,305 arrivals recorded on 3 September 2022.Last week, a record 165 migrants arrived in a single boat.Additional reporting by Dan Wainwright, BBC Verify

schema.headline: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year

title: Michael Vaughan: England Test captaincy could be 'exactly what Joe Root needs'
description: Former skipper Michael Vaughan has said the England Test captaincy could be "exactly what Joe Root needs".Speaking on the Test Match Special podcast,
body: Former skipper Michael Vaughan has said the England Test captaincy could be "exactly what Joe Root needs".Speaking on the Test Match Special podcast, Vaughan said the 35-year-old's return to the role, having led the team from 2017 to 2022, might prove to be motivation in the later stages of his career."I just wonder from Joe's perspective if he needed this to get that real enthusiasm to get up every morning to play Test match cricket," said Vaughan."The amount of cricket that he's played, I just wonder whether he needed this little trigger, this little motivational tool."He hasn't got that many of his close friends in the team any more, a lot of his team-mates have retired or moved on, so maybe this is exactly what Joe Root needs as well."Root returns to the captaincy under the charge of interim head coach Marcus Trescothick after Brendon McCullum was sacked, before New Zealander Stephen Fleming takes over the Test leadership for this winter's tour of South Africa.He stepped down as captain in 2022 after a 10-wicket loss to West Indies, their ninth match without a win, citing the "toll" and "impact" the role had on him.However, Vaughan stated he believed Root had been dealt a "dodgy hand" during his time as Test captain."Around the time he was appointed England were trying to win the 50-over World Cup and all the England eggs were put in the white-ball basket," said Vaughan."Then Covid struck. None of us would know how hard it would be to captain in a Covid time - Joe had to do that. "That Caribbean tour where it came to an end, it looked like a job that was a little bit too far for him. He's a little bit older, a little bit wiser. I think Stephen Fleming will help out with a lot of the stuff that some captains get drained by - organising the dressing room and making sure the tactical side of the team is in good order."I just think in terms of his motivation and in terms of what is left for Joe Root to achieve in the game, of course there's a few runs to get past Sachin [Tendulkar's all-time Test run-scoring record] but if he can be an Ashes winner next year, a world leader in runs he's scored in Test cricket, you can't ask for a more perfect career."Fleming has been appointed on a four-year deal that will mean he coaches England in the next two Ashes series, and Vaughan said managing director Rob Key has selected a "very experienced" option.Former England Test coach Andy Flower was initially linked with the role, but Royal Challengers Bengaluru and London Spirit coach ruled himself out of the process.Fleming joins after leaving Chennai Super Kings this month, having coached the Indian Premier League (IPL) franchise for the past nine seasons."Andy Flower, I think from what I've read is the one that they wanted. He turned that down so it was like 'OK, how do we get the next best?'" Vaughan said of Fleming."Some will say he's not coached in red-ball cricket but you've got a very experienced manager, very experienced coach who's been around the modern game with Chennai Super Kings over the course of the last few years. "He was a very, very good captain back in the day, a very good tactician, renowned for being a really good man-manager. "Having McCullum still as the white-ball coach and then having someone coaching the Test team who doesn't know McCullum, that could have been really tricky. "I think Stephen Fleming has been brought in for that reason - he's obviously very close to McCullum. "They needed someone who could work with McCullum because someone that doesn't know Baz and his style, I think it could have got very, very messy."Fleming, who retired from playing in 2009, has a wealth of experience in Test cricket, making 111 appearances for New Zealand, scoring 7,172 runs with an average of 40.06 in the middle order.McCullum was known for promoting an aggressive form of cricket, dubbed Bazball by fans and the media, but Vaughan said Fleming will have to make changes to England's style and technique."I'm kind of sick and tired of talking about England's style of play. The style of play I want to see is England winning," Vaughan added. "Whatever that style is on that given day, session, hour, England have to play the right style of cricket that wins games of cricket. "We can only talk about talent and the gulf of talent in English cricket for so long - they've got to start winning games of cricket and winning trophies now."The one thing this Test team needs is coaching the technical side of batting. "How many of them can look themselves in the mirror and when Michael Neser, Matt Henry, Scott Boland bowls that good length just on or around that off stump, can play a controlled forward defence shot? "They won't like saying it and they won't like talking about technique, but technique wins Test match cricket and the technical side of England's players and batting has been found wanting. "So it's all right putting a good leader of the group, but I also think they need one or two changes in the backroom team to make sure these players are getting really well coached as well."

schema.headline: Michael Vaughan: England Test captaincy could be 'exactly what Joe Root needs'

title: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
description: The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on Ameri
body: The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on American forces.Centcom said it hit "dozens" of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in response to Iran's firing on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.Iranian state media said the latest strikes had killed three people, including a two-year-old child, on Qeshm island, while other locations were also hit in the south and west of the country.The latest hostilities come on a week that has seen the conflict expand, with the first publicly announced joint US-Saudi strikes targeting Iranian proxies in Iraq.Iran and the US have engaged in escalating strikes and counter-strikes since a ceasefire in April, aimed at pausing the months-long war, fell apart in June. The US has blockaded Iranian ports and bombed Iranian sites, while Iran has fired missiles and drones at US assets in countries across the Middle East and targeted shipping in the economically important Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf and Arabian Sea.On Wednesday, news outlet Axios cited an unnamed US official as saying that Trump had met Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, who had conveyed that Saudi Arabia wants to de-escalate tensions. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Analysis: Saudi Arabia's dilemma as it tries to stay out of US-Iran warMeanwhile, the Egyptian government said a fire at a port on Wednesday had been caused by a drone attack. Egypt, a US ally, has not previously been directly attacked during the war.The US-Iran conflict has reignited after several days of relative calm.For days, both sides halted strikes as talks apparently restarted in hopes of some type of diplomatic solution. Trump called them "very friendly negotiations", though Tehran denied any discussions were happening. But following the Iranian missile attack on a US base in Jordan on Tuesday, Trump vowed to retaliate, telling reporters at the White House: "We're going to be hitting them very hard because it's our turn to hit them.  They know it's coming. They asked us not to do it."The latest wave of US strikes started at 20:00 ET on Wednesday (01:00 BST on Thursday) and lasted about an hour, with Centcom calling them a "powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East". All of Iran's missiles were intercepted, Centcom said. The attack by the US targeted "military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities," Centcom wrote once the strikes were complete.Iranian state media agency Irib reported that the islands of Qeshm and Abadan, both central to the oil industry, were among the areas hit.  "A US attack on a residential home in the Chah Tangu neighbourhood of Qeshm killed three members of a family: the father, the mother, and their 2-year-old child," Fars reported citing the Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences.A man in his 30s living in the south of the island told BBC Persian he was heading to Tehran, because "things are becoming more dangerous here"."Our internet situation has been a mess. The electricity has been cutting out several times since this morning," he said. "There have been loud bangs since 03:40 this morning. We are helpless."Meanwhile, Jordan's armed forces said that air defence systems had successfully shot down five Iranian missiles targeting the Kingdom's territory on Thursday.On Tuesday, the IRGC said it had targeted a US air base and a command centre in Jordan "in response to the acts of aggression of the American child-killing army".It also said naval forces had struck three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they "ignored warnings" and sailed along what it described as an "unsafe and illegal route" through the vital Gulf waterway.Last Friday, Trump suspended an intensive bombing campaign that had lasted for 13 consecutive nights. The US said it had targeted Iranian weapons and military sites. Scores of people were reported to have died.On Tuesday, Centcom said the joint US-Saudi strikes hit "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours".Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which is dominated by Iran-backed Shia militias, said at least 20 of its members had been killed in US-Saudi strikes on its bases.The Iraqi presidency said it denounced the bombing of the PMF bases, calling it "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty".But Trump told Fox News the strikes had been "co-ordinated with the Iraqi government".Saudi Arabia, which sees itself as the leading Sunni Muslim power, and Iran, the largest Shia Muslim country, have been locked in a struggle for regional dominance for decades.With additional reporting from Ghoncheh Habibiazad, BBC Persian

schema.headline: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops

title: Dad of Mersea beach tragedy victim pays tribute to his son
description: A seven-year-old boy who died a week after being rescued from the sea "never failed to bring happiness" to others, his father has told the BBC.Musa Ah
body: A seven-year-old boy who died a week after being rescued from the sea "never failed to bring happiness" to others, his father has told the BBC.Musa Ahmed and five relatives got into difficulty in the water in West Mersea on 22 July, having travelled to the Essex seaside from east London.His 15-year-old cousin, Sameeha Rahman, and her mother Shelina, 41, drowned at the scene.Shahin Ahmed said his son was "a unique and happy personality, a sphere of joy" in a tribute after his death on Tuesday evening."Everyone who knew him had a unique relationship with him. He made every person feel special and never failed to bring happiness," Ahmed said."He was everyone's favourite and he made everyone feel like his favourite."Ahmed also referred to Islam and said Musa "embodied" traits of the Prophet Muhammad.

schema.headline: Dad of Mersea beach tragedy victim pays tribute to his son

title: Former England football star Shaun Wright-Phillips joins Strictly 2026 line-up
description: Former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.The footb
body: Former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.The football pundit, who is the son of Arsenal legend Ian Wright, had 36 caps for England and also played for clubs including Chelsea and Queens Park Rangers.His fancy footwork may have dazzled on the pitch but Wright-Phillips says this latest challenge "is definitely outside my comfort zone. Dancing is in my blood -but mainly at family events! I'm super excited to get started and really looking forward to the challenge!"While ex-footballers have had mixed fortunes on previous Strictly series, former soccer star Karen Carney flipped the script last year by winning the coveted glitterball.Wright-Phillips is the tenth celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including  Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer and Jaime Winstone.More celebrities are set to be announced in the coming weeks, with 15 expected in the final line-up.Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition. The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me"."I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year. Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton is also part of this year's line-up.Appleton, best known for his work with Kim Kardashian, joins singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem, EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and reality star Dani Dyer in the battle for the Glitterball trophy.The Leicester-born Color Wow creative director said: "I'm thrilled to be joining Strictly Come Dancing and coming home to the UK for this incredible experience."He has also created red carpet looks for the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, while having his work showcased on the covers of publications including Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Vanity Fair."I've always believed that the best things happen when you take a chance and try something new," added the 43-year-old, who this year released a memoir entitled Your Roots Don't Define You."I may know my way around a salon floor, but the dance floor is a whole different story - and I can't wait to get started."Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.The first line-up announcements were made significantly earlier than usual - the BBC usually confirms the line-up in August.  Speaking to ITV's Good Morning Britain in June, Ballas said: "There are going to be some people on there that will make you go 'wow'."Asked about the new presenting trio, Ballas said she was "very excited to see what they bring" to the show. "I know they took lots of chemistry tests, as did everybody, and those chemistry tests have brought those three people together, and I believe it's absolutely unbelievable," she said.Ballas described the number of new elements on this year's show as "quite extraordinary", but added that it will still feel familiar to viewers."I don't think they'll change the show too much, maybe tweaks here and there, but no major changes."Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

schema.headline: Former England football star Shaun Wright-Phillips joins Strictly 2026 line-up

title: Greek police probe 'foul play' in death of woman found in suitcase
description: Image source, FacebookImage caption, A photo of Elisabeth-Jane Ross which appeared to have been taken in 2015ByMary McCoolBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours
body: Image source, FacebookImage caption, A photo of Elisabeth-Jane Ross which appeared to have been taken in 2015ByMary McCoolBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoGreek police have said they are trying to determine whether foul play was involved in the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase.Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, reportedly by a homeless man.She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found and is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus two weeks before her death.A spokesperson for police in Greece told the BBC: "We are awaiting the results of the toxicology tests to determine the cause of death and ascertain whether foul play was involved, as this was not clarified by the initial examination of the body."Image source, EUROKINISSIImage caption, Greek police at the scene in the Kypseli district in AthensFirst Minister John Swinney said Ross's family would be supported by the Scottish government and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.He said: "This is an absolutely appalling case that has been reported overnight."And obviously I'm deeply concerned that such a tragedy has taken place."Helena Smith, The Guardian's correspondent in Athens, told BBC Radio Scotland that the body was found in a derelict building in downtown Athens, "in an area that is booming, full of Airbnbs".She said: "It is very popular with people travelling through Athens and young foreigners who have elected to make the Greek capital their home."Smith said that Ross had family in Edinburgh and "connections" to Greece - staying with a friend in Athens before she disappeared.She added: "It would seem that someone had control over her mobile phone after she died and was sending messages to distract the authorities and close friends from trying to track her down."Image caption, Elisabeth-Jane Ross was found in the Kypseli district of AthensOn Wednesday the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed they were providing consular support and were in contact with the Greek authorities.A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We are aware of the death of Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece."Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland."Interpol said it was not able to comment on individual cases.

schema.headline: Greek police probe 'foul play' in death of woman found in suitcase

title: Drought declared for whole of Wales amid sustained high temperatures
description: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'Image source, EPABySteffan MessengerWales environment correspondent and Oliver SlowB
body: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'Image source, EPABySteffan MessengerWales environment correspondent and Oliver SlowBBC WalesA drought has been extended across the whole of Wales with the country on course for its driest July on record in 190 years.Declaring the drought, the country's environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate".The decision has been made in response to record-low river levels, dry soils, widespread wildfires and mounting impacts on wildlife, farming and forestry.NRW had already announced a drought across the north and parts of mid Wales last week.Image source, Tudur DaviesImage caption, The lack of rain in Wales has led to low water levels in reservoirs like Llyn Aled Isaf in Conwy last weekThe nationwide announcement made on Thursday will trigger more monitoring of rivers and stronger advice for the public on use of water.The declaration of a drought does not mean there is currently a threat to water supplies for homes and businesses, with Welsh water companies saying reservoir levels are holding up after a wet start to the year.NRW said figures had shown Wales had received 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, with most rivers in the country "exceptionally low".Groundwater levels are also falling in Wales, with some lower than expected for the time of year.The environmental body said its teams were dealing with reports of "wide-reaching impacts to the environment", and that "conditions across Wales' natural environment have continued to deteriorate".This includes drying riverbeds, fish in distress, an accumulation of algae, wildfire risk and concern from farmers about crop growth, grazing conditions and water availability for livestock.Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / NadzenaImage caption, Parched land has been seen across much of Wales this week, including in this park in Dinas Powys, Vale of GlamorganRhian Thomas, from NRW, said the toll from the recent dry weather had been "clear to see", and teams were closely monitoring forecasts and river flows."With no strong indications for notable rainfall in the forecasts, and risks of further heatwaves over the summer, it's more important than ever that we all use water wisely," she said."Every drop we waste is less water for our rivers and wildlife when they need it the most."The dry weather in recent weeks has also coincided with a number of wildfires across Wales.A fire that broke out earlier this month in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd could be seen from space, with a firefighting helicopter deployed to tackle the blaze.Residents were evacuated from their homes following a fire close to Conwy Mountain said they had heard the blaze, which had sounded "like popcorn", coming down the mountain.First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said he had organised a summit to look at the risks of fires from severe droughts.Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, he said while there was no "immediate risk to the provision of drinking water", there needed to be "more resilience in our water supplies" across Wales and the UK.Image caption, George Tomlinson says the dry weather makes him worry about the future of farmingGeorge Tomlinson, 29, who runs Rossett Park Farming in Wrexham, said he had to sell 60 cows because the drought had killed off grazing land."There's nothing available for the cows to eat on the grazing platform apart from a little bit of dead grass some dry cows are eating," said Tomlinson, adding "you've got to make tough decisions in order to survive".He said he was also worried about what the future might hold with warmer summers expected."If this continues a lot of farmers will be forced to close their gates and never open them again," he said, describing it as "depressing". Image caption, Farmer Richard Anthony says his land is as hard as a "rock" and has "no moisture at all"Richard Anthony, whose farm stretches over the Vale of Glamorgan and Bridgend county, said the ground on his land was as hard as a "rock" and had "no moisture at all".The dry land has left Anthony unable to plant his crops, who added he had "never ever been in this situation" before."As soon as we've harvested the one crop, we plant in the next crop, but we can't do any of that now," he said. "I've never seen it as bad as this."Our wheat deals are down between 20% and 30%. That is massive. we'll have to cope, we will survive, but the knock-on effect is huge."Anthony said he is concerned that once the rain comes it will not  stop, leaving him unable to plant next year's crops."It'll go from this to being too wet", he added.National Farmers Union Cymru president Abi Reader has warned that the cost of the continuing dry and hot weather will have a financial impact on farmers."We're going to see costs for these farms rising, because they might be having to buy in extra feed for their livestock, or they might be spending a lot of money carting water," she said."We've been in this a long time now, and it's going to take a long time to recover, and absolutely everybody needs to remember that food security starts with water security," she added.What is a drought?A drought occurs when a prolonged lack of rainfall and high temperatures causes severe stress to natural ecosystems.NRW says it results in critically low river and groundwater levels as well as dry soils - which has an impact on wildlife, fisheries and protected habitats.It also has impacts for farming and forestry - such as failing crops - while private water supplies like natural springs and boreholes can run dry.A declaration of environmental drought triggers more monitoring of rivers and releases from reservoirs to help top up the flow.Those who have licences to take water from rivers - from farms and canals to golf courses - will face restrictions.There's a big communications element to this too - so it means firmer advice for the public on using water wisely.There is a difference between NRW's drought announcements and those made by water companies.Welsh Water already have a hosepipe ban in place for parts of west Wales as a result of unprecedented demand during the recent heatwaves, making it harder to process and deliver enough water around the network.But they say there is currently no threat to drinking water supplies and reservoir levels are holding up.

schema.headline: Drought declared for whole of Wales amid sustained high temperatures

title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
description: The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.In a major blow to the H
body: The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than £1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year. Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the  home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.During Thursday, some 117 protesters were arrested outside Westminster Magistrates' Court, with Metropolitan Police saying the majority of arrests were for expressing support for the group.Scores of protesters had turned up there because they had expected to appear in court accused of allegedly showing support for the group at earlier public events. However, those cases had been listed in error. Many of the defendants said that they felt they had no choice but to turn up, despite the court and Metropolitan Police telling them not to do so. Palestine Action co-founder Ammori welcomed the Supreme Court's decision to hear her appeal - and said that the latest arrests were part of a wider crackdown on Palestinian solidarity."We will continue to fight this proscription all the way to the Supreme Court and, if necessary, to the European Court of Human Rights to overturn what has become one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history."The Home Office has repeatedly said that the ban of the group has nothing to do with protest in support of Palestinian causes - and was necessary because it was causing significant criminal damage to legitimate businesses.Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal have ruled that Palestine Action's activities include criminal acts - although they were divided on whether those incidents justified turning to terrorism laws.Those laws - approved by MPs in Parliament - allow the government to ban a group for either serious violence or serious criminal damage for an ideological cause - and trigger wider powers for the police to investigate and charge suspects for organising activities and fundraising.The Home Office has been contacted for comment but following its major win at the Court of Appeal it said that it would robustly defend any further appeal to the Supreme Court. The BBC understands that position has not altered since the change in prime minister.

schema.headline: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court

title: Eddie Howe: Does Newcastle manager's departure mark the beginning of the end of Saudi dream?
description: Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when his side won the Carabao Cup last year.But rumours about the 48-year-old's departure ha
body: Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when his side won the Carabao Cup last year.But rumours about the 48-year-old's departure have been circulating since the beginning of this year, when Newcastle sat 13th in the Premier League and securing Champions League football for next season was already starting to look highly unlikely.That was exacerbated further in March when the Magpies were struck by a late Sunderland comeback in the Tyne-Wear derby, losing 2-1 at St James' Park, to extend their dismal league record against their local rivals to 15 years without victory.They also went out of the FA Cup in the fifth round, exited the Champions League in the last 16 and made it to the semi-finals of the EFL Cup only to be beaten 5-1 by Manchester City over two legs.Despite that, Howe's four-and-a-half-year stint as Newcastle boss will be looked back on fondly by Newcastle fans. What supporters will perhaps be most perplexed by is the timing of Howe's departure.The former Bournemouth boss could have left at the end of the season and would probably have been given a positive send off by fans.Indeed, BBC Sport understands potential replacements for Howe were sounded out in July, including Kieran McKenna.So what are the rules that Newcastle have, at times, come close to breaking?From the beginning of the PIF takeover, Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) have put the brakes on Newcastle's ambitions to spend.Just because a club has wealthy owners does not mean they can spend big in the transfer windows.After buying the club in 2021, PIF spent £404.7m in the first three years. But by bringing in only £50.4m from sales, Newcastle saw the stark reality of PSR hit home in 2024.That led to them having to sell homegrown talent Elliot Anderson to Nottingham Forest and has snowballed since, with important players being offloaded every season.The Magpies welcomed the new Financial Fair Play rules - the Squad Cost Ratio (SCR), which are now in effect - and, in short, mean the more you generate, the more you can spend.But, when analysing their spending power against that of other Premier League clubs, Swiss Ramble, external found that the Magpies' SCR budget ranked ninth (£243m) in the Premier League.On top of that, in April the PIF withdrew its multibillion dollar backing of LIV Golf after Yasir Al-Rumayyan - the fund's governor and chairman of Newcastle - confirmed the PIF was reviewing its deals and investments.In turn, questions were raised about what that meant for the future of Newcastle - but senior club figures were informed at the time that the pullout did not affect the club. The fund is still viewed as being engaged.In the club's most recent set of accounts from last season, Newcastle's revenues have more than doubled to £335.3m - from the £140.2m recorded in the final full campaign of Mike Ashley's ownership.There are also plans for a new state-of-the-art training ground while Hopkinson has outlined a desire to revamp St James' Park or move stadiums to increase matchday revenue.The potential appointment of former RB Salzburg boss Jaissle is also intriguing given he is currently in charge of Saudi Arabian side Al-Ahli - a club the PIF held a majority stake in until selling it in April.

schema.headline: Eddie Howe: Does Newcastle manager's departure mark the beginning of the end of Saudi dream?
